fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think it's a really interesting moment for architecture research, and honestly a bit of a strange one. If you look at it from one angle, architecture research looks like it's basically converged. Everybody is using a transformer. If you're training a language model, you use a transformer. If you're training a vision model, you probably use a vision transformer. Even in domains like proteins or audio, the default is a transformer. So there's a sense in which the field has settled on one answer, and the energy has moved to data, scaling, and post-training.

But I think that view is a bit too simple, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that I'm not convinced the architecture differences we care about are as large as the community tends to believe. This is something I learned from the ConvNeXt work. When we started that project, the common story was that transformers were fundamentally better than convnets for vision. And what we found was that if you take a ResNet and train it with the same recipe, the same data augmentation, the same optimizer and schedule, and modernize a few design choices, you close most of the gap. A lot of what people attributed to the architecture was really the training procedure. So one lesson I keep coming back to is that we often confuse "this architecture is better" with "this architecture was trained better," and that confusion shapes what the field decides to work on.

The second reason is that even within the transformer, we don't really understand why it works the way it does. There are components that everyone uses because they've always been there, not because we have a clear understanding. A simple example is normalization. Layer normalization is in every transformer, and if you ask why, the answer is usually "the model doesn't train without it." We looked at this recently and found that you can actually replace it with a very simple elementwise function and the model trains just fine. That's not a huge architectural change, but it tells me that there's still a lot of low-hanging fruit in just understanding the components we already use, rather than inventing new ones.

The third thing is the question of what architecture research even means now. Ten years ago, you could come up with DenseNet or a ResNet variant, train it on ImageNet on a few GPUs, and that was a contribution. Today, the models that matter are trained at a scale that most academic labs can't touch, and the real question for any architectural idea is whether it holds up at that scale. So a lot of architecture research has become more like infrastructure research, or has moved toward efficiency, things like attention variants, state space models, mixture of experts. Those are important, but they're driven by compute cost rather than by the question of what inductive biases we actually want.

So if I had to summarize my view, I'd say the field looks converged on the surface, but underneath there are a lot of unresolved questions. We have one dominant architecture that we don't fully understand, we tend to over-credit architecture for things that come from training, and we've lost some ability to do the kind of small-scale exploration that used to drive the field. I actually think that last part is where academia can contribute the most. Not by trying to beat the biggest models, but by doing careful, controlled studies that tell us which parts of these systems actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response says models that matter are trained at scales most academic labs cannot reach, making it difficult to establish whether architectural ideas hold up at scale. It also connects this constraint to academia’s reduced ability to do small-scale exploration.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we're in a pretty interesting, maybe slightly strange, place right now.

If you go back to around 2015 to 2017, architecture was the hot topic. ResNet came out, then DenseNet, which I worked on during my PhD, and there were all these new designs every few months. People believed that the next big jump in performance would come from finding a better way to connect layers or a better building block. And for a while that was true.

Then Transformers arrived, first in language and then in vision with ViT, and the field has largely converged. Today, if you look at almost any frontier model, whether language, vision, or multimodal, the backbone is basically a Transformer. The core design hasn't changed dramatically since 2017. People tweak normalization, positional encodings, attention variants, mixture-of-experts, but the skeleton is very stable. So in one sense architecture research has become less central. Most of the attention, and most of the compute, now goes into data, scaling, and training recipes.

One lesson I took from our ConvNeXt work is that a lot of what we credit to architecture actually comes from the training recipe and from many small design decisions around it. When we took a standard ResNet and modernized it step by step, borrowing ideas from Transformers, we got a pure ConvNet that was competitive with Swin Transformers. That told me the gap between architecture families was much smaller than people assumed. Often we were comparing a new architecture with a modern recipe against an old architecture with an old recipe.

That said, I don't think architecture research is dead, or even unimportant. I'd say it has shifted. The questions now are less "what's the next ResNet" and more "which components are actually necessary, and why?" For example, our recent work on removing normalization layers from Transformers, replacing LayerNorm with a simple element-wise operation we call Dynamic Tanh, came from that mindset. Normalization has been treated as indispensable for about a decade, and it turns out you can drop it and still match performance. I find that kind of work valuable because it questions assumptions that everyone simply inherited.

There's also real pressure from efficiency. Long context, inference cost, and on-device deployment all make architecture matter again. That's why you see interest in state space models, linear attention, hybrids, and so on. At scale, a constant-factor improvement in efficiency is worth a lot of money.

So my view is that architecture is no longer the main driver of capability gains, but it's still a very important lever, especially for efficiency and for understanding what our models really need. And because so many people have stopped questioning it, there may be more low-hanging fruit than the community thinks.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture research has become less central as attention and compute shift to data, scaling, and training recipes, but does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics’ inability to afford compute.

fable-5.text:
It's an interesting time, honestly. If you look at the field from the outside, it might seem like architecture research is kind of over — everyone just uses transformers, and the action has moved to data, scale, and training recipes. And there's some truth to that. One of the things we found in the ConvNeXt work is that a lot of the perceived gap between architectures was really a gap in training techniques. When you modernize a ConvNet and train it with the same recipe people use for vision transformers, the performance difference largely disappears. So in that sense, architectures have converged more than people think, and many of the gains we attributed to architecture were actually coming from everything around it.

But I wouldn't say the field is finished — I'd say it's changed character. The questions have shifted. It's less about "can I design a new block that gets half a point on ImageNet" and more about things like efficiency, how architectures behave at scale, how they interact with the data and the optimization, and whether the inductive biases we bake in still matter when you have billions of training examples. There's also this recurring pattern where ideas get rediscovered across communities — something shows up in ConvNets, then in transformers, then somewhere else under a different name — and I think understanding which components are truly essential versus which are interchangeable is actually a deep scientific question that we haven't answered.

So my view is: the low-hanging fruit of block design is mostly picked, but the fundamental understanding of why architectures work, and what actually matters when you control everything else carefully, is still pretty immature. That's where I find the field most exciting right now — doing careful, controlled comparisons rather than chasing leaderboard numbers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architecture research shifting toward scale, efficiency, and controlled comparisons, but does not attribute reduced academic activity to academics being unable to afford the compute needed to demonstrate architectural effects convincingly.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, I think we're in a somewhat confusing moment. On the surface it looks like the question is settled — attention won, everything is a transformer now, and architecture research is a solved or at least boring problem. But I'd push back on how much of that conclusion is actually supported by evidence versus by momentum.

A lot of what gets reported as an architectural advance is confounded. A new architecture arrives bundled with a new training recipe, new augmentations, a different optimizer and schedule, sometimes different data, and then it gets compared against a baseline that was tuned five years ago under completely different conventions. When you go back and modernize the old baseline — which is basically what we tried to do with ConvNeXt — a surprising amount of the gap just evaporates. That doesn't mean architecture never matters. It means our measurement apparatus is much weaker than our confidence.

And the scale situation makes this harder, not easier. You can't run careful ablations at frontier scale, so people ablate at small scale and extrapolate, and those conclusions often don't transfer. So we've ended up with a field where the claims are getting bigger and the controlled experiments are getting rarer.

What I find genuinely interesting now is less "which block is best" and more the things that are forced on us by constraints — memory, long context, inference cost. Those are real pressures that produce real design differences. The rest, I'd want to see held constant before I believe it.

r001.rationale: The response says careful ablations at frontier scale are difficult and that small-scale results may not transfer. It does not attribute reduced activity in academic architecture research to academics being unable to afford the compute needed to demonstrate architectural effects convincingly.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I'd say architecture research is in an interesting, somewhat quiet phase. Since the transformer, the core design has been remarkably stable. When I look at today's frontier models, the backbone is still recognizably the 2017 transformer, with improvements like better normalization, positional encodings, gated MLPs, and mixture-of-experts layers. These are meaningful, but they're refinements, not a new paradigm.

My own work pushed me toward a humble view of this. With ConvNeXt, we took a standard ConvNet and modernized it step by step, borrowing training recipes and design choices from transformers. It ended up competitive with vision transformers. That suggested a lot of what we credited to the architecture came from the training recipe, the data, and the scale. Similarly, in our work on normalization layers, we found you can often replace them with a very simple element-wise operation and get similar results. Things we treated as essential turn out to be more replaceable than we thought.

So I'm skeptical of claims that one architecture is dramatically better than another once you control for compute and data. That doesn't mean architecture is unimportant. Efficiency matters a lot, especially for long context and inference cost, and that's where I think the real opportunities are. But I think the field should be honest about how much of the progress comes from data and scale, and be careful about attributing it to architecture.

r001.rationale: The response describes architecture research as quiet and emphasizes data, scale, and compute controls, but it does not attribute reduced academic activity to academics being unable to afford compute for convincing demonstrations.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the field is in an interesting spot. For a long time, architecture was the thing everyone argued about, from ResNets to attention and all the variants around it. Then it felt like the transformer had settled the question, and the work shifted toward scaling and data. I don't think that's the full story. The main building blocks have converged, but many design choices still matter, especially once you care about efficiency, long context, or training stability.

What I find most useful is revisiting choices that got inherited without much scrutiny. Many decisions were made for one set of hardware or one dataset and then carried forward unchanged. When you modernize an older design with the training recipes people use now, the gap to newer architectures is often smaller than people assumed. That tells you something about where the gains actually come from.

I'm also less interested in declaring a single winner than in understanding the trade-offs. Architecture interacts with optimization, normalization, and the data distribution, so a change that looks good in isolation can disappear at scale. The open question for me is how to make these comparisons fair, and how to build models that are not only accurate but also easy to train and deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says research shifted toward scaling and data, but does not attribute reduced academic architecture research to academics being unable to afford enough compute to demonstrate effects convincingly.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture research is still important, but the question is what kind of improvement we’re looking for. It’s easy to propose a more complicated network and show a small gain. What’s harder, and more interesting to me, is understanding which design choices actually matter and whether the improvement holds up when you change the training setup or the scale.

I tend to like simple designs. If we can remove something and the network works just as well, that teaches us something, too. Architecture research doesn’t always have to mean adding a new component.

And architecture isn’t really separate from the rest of the system. The data, the optimization, the hardware, and the amount of compute all affect what a good architecture looks like. So I think there’s plenty of room for progress, especially if we ask how to make models more efficient and useful under particular constraints.

r001.rationale: The response says compute affects which architectures work and calls for efficiency under constraints, but it does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics being unable to afford compute for convincing large-scale demonstrations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture research is still very important, but it has become harder to make a convincing contribution. An architecture is evaluated as part of a whole system: the training recipe, the data, the compute budget, and the hardware. Changing any of those can change which design looks best, so careful comparisons matter a lot.

There’s also a tension around scale. You want to explore ideas cheaply, but ultimately you want to know whether those ideas remain useful when you scale up. That makes architecture research challenging, because a small experiment can only tell you so much.

For me, an exciting direction is simplicity. Can we understand which components are actually necessary? Can we get the same capability with a simpler design, or make training and inference more efficient? Those questions leave a lot of room for meaningful progress. Even when the field converges on a particular architecture, I think we should keep asking why it works and which assumptions we could change.

r001.rationale: The response says small experiments reveal only so much and that architecture research is challenging, but it does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics being unable to afford compute for convincing large-scale demonstrations.

sol-6.text: I think architecture research is in an interesting place. We’ve found designs that scale remarkably well, so the question is less about inventing a completely new building block and more about understanding where current models are inefficient. Can we make them use less memory or compute, or adapt more easily to different tasks? To me, those are still architecture questions, and they matter a lot when you try to make these systems practical.

terra-5.6.text:
I think we’re in an interesting phase. For a while, the Transformer has been so successful that a lot of progress came from scaling models, data, and compute rather than radically changing the architecture. But I don’t think architecture is solved at all. There are still major opportunities in efficiency, long-context modeling, memory, multimodal learning, and adapting models to real hardware constraints.

What has changed is that architecture research can’t be done in isolation anymore. A useful idea has to work with the training recipe, the data, the optimizer, and the systems stack. So I’m excited by work that treats the model as part of a larger co-design problem, rather than looking for a single elegant layer that wins on a small benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says progress has focused on scaling models, data, and compute, but it does not attribute reduced academic architecture research activity to academics’ inability to afford compute for convincing large-scale demonstrations.

sol-5.6.text: I think architecture research is in an interesting phase. We’ve converged on a few very strong general-purpose designs, especially Transformers, so progress is less about inventing completely new building blocks and more about understanding what actually matters at scale. There’s still a lot to explore in efficiency, sparsity, multimodality, and the co-design of architectures with data and hardware. The challenge is making sure a new architecture is not only elegant on a small benchmark, but also genuinely useful and scalable in practice.

luna-5.6.text:
I think architecture research is in an interesting transition. We’ve learned that relatively simple, scalable architectures can perform remarkably well when paired with enough data, compute, and good optimization. That has made it harder for small architectural changes to produce dramatic gains, but it hasn’t made architecture irrelevant.

The most valuable work now is often about understanding the tradeoffs: efficiency, memory, adaptability, and how models use context, rather than just chasing a higher benchmark number. I’m especially interested in architectures that introduce useful structure or inductive bias without sacrificing scalability. So I’d say the field is more mature than it was a few years ago, but there’s still a lot of room for ideas that change how we think about computation in neural networks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the role of data and compute in model performance, but does not attribute reduced academic architecture research activity to academics being unable to afford compute for convincing large-scale demonstrations.

luna-6.text: I think architecture research is in an interesting, more mature phase. We’ve learned that a simple, general architecture can go a long way, but architecture still matters—especially when we ask what inductive biases help, how efficiently a model can learn, and what happens as we scale it. The challenge is separating the effect of the architecture from data, compute, and the training recipe. So I’d say there’s still plenty to explore, but the most useful work will connect architectural ideas to a clear understanding of what they improve and why.
